HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e114.summary: Title rubric for the fourth question of the Prologue: whether the theology of the wayfarer is properly called affective.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e125.summary: States the question — whether the science of sacred Scripture is properly called affective — with the principal argument against: no science, being an intellectual habit, should be named from an act of the will, and affection is an act of the will.
claims: An intellectual habit should not be named from an act of the will.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e141.summary: Argument to the contrary: a science is properly called affective that not only illumines the intellect but per se and properly affects and delights the affect; theology does so.
claims: Theology illumines the intellect and also per se affects and delights the affect.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e151.summary: Divides the question into four articles: from what a science is properly named; given that it is named from its end, what theology's proper end is; the question itself (whether theology is affective); and the removal of motives of various opinions opposing the truth stated in Article 3.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e177.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio': every science is named from its proper end; since the proper end of theology is the love of God, sacred theology should be called affective, or rather dilective.
claims: A science is named from its proper end.
Since the love of God is theology's proper end, theology is affective or dilective.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e193.summary: Article heading and question: from what a science is properly named.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e204.summary: Reports the view of some that a science should be properly named from its object.
claims: Some hold that a science is named from its object.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e208.summary: First argument for naming from the object: a habit should be named from that from which it per se derives its species and entity, and habits are specified by their objects.
claims: Habits are specified by their objects and so should be named from them.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e217.summary: Second argument: a habit is named from what distinguishes it from all others, since distinction and denomination go together; habits are distinguished by objects, since powers are distinguished by acts and acts by objects (De anima 2), and sciences are divided as their things are (De anima 3).
claims: Habits are distinguished, and so named, by their objects.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e239.summary: Thomas rejects this: if sciences were named from objects, there could not be two sciences of one object, one simply practical and the other simply speculative; but a human's moral science of the virtues is practical, while an angel's science of the same virtues is speculative. With Aristotle he holds that a science is named from its end: in Metaph. 2 he proves first philosophy speculative because the end of speculative science is truth and of practical science work, and Averroes calls this proof manifest, which it would not be if the proper cause were the object. Further, the same science can be practical or speculative depending on the end to which a knower refers it, as even the opponents concede.
claims: Sciences are properly named from their ends, not their objects.
The same object can be treated by a practical and a speculative science.
Aristotle distinguishes speculative and practical sciences by their ends, truth and work.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e304.summary: Fourth argument: when two causes concur in an effect, one depending on the other but not conversely, the effect is more properly named from the independent cause (provided it is no less proper and determinate — added to block objections about universal causes like God or the sun); object and end concur in causing a habit, and the object depends on the end, since it causes as an efficient cause moved by the goodness of the end, the end being the cause of causes (Physics 2).
claims: An effect is better named from the independent of two concurring causes.
The object depends on the end in causing a habit, since the end is the cause of causes.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e343.summary: Further argument: Aristotle in De anima 3 says the speculative differs from the practical by its end.
claims: The speculative and practical differ by their end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e345.summary: Further argument: even the object is named from the end, being called speculable because its end is to be speculated; so the habit is principally named from the end.
claims: Objects themselves are named from ends, so habits are a fortiori named from ends.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e363.summary: Further argument: the same health can be considered by the natural philosopher, whose science is speculative because he intends only speculation, and by the physician, whose science is practical because he intends to act.
claims: The same object yields speculative or practical science according to the end intended.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e376.summary: Further argument: a habit should be named from the cause from whose causality it can in no way be absolved rather than from one it can be absolved from without contradiction; God can create a science through an ideal ratio, supplying the object's efficient causality, but the science cannot be absolved from the intention of the end, since without intending speculation it would not be speculative, nor practical without intending work.
claims: God can supply the efficient causality of the object but a science cannot be separated from its end.
Hence a science is more properly named from its end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e392.summary: Anticipated reply: God can absolve the habit from the object as efficient cause but not as terminating cause, since a speculative science must terminate in a speculable object. Thomas rejects this: the habit in its whole entity pre-exists its terminus, and the object does not cause the habit insofar as it terminates it, so the habit can be absolved from all the object's causality.
claims: A habit pre-exists its terminus and is not caused by the object as terminating it.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e424.summary: Further argument: naming should be principally from what determines all other causes according to its requirement, and the end does so (Grosseteste: all else is moderated and measured by the end's requirement). Authorities seeming to say otherwise mean that though sciences are distinguished and named in some way by objects, they are so per se and principally by ends.
claims: The end determines all other causes and so is the principal source of a science's name.
Authorities naming sciences from objects should be read as secondary.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e438.summary: Objection: how does the end name the science? Either as acquired (but then it is posterior to the habit and cannot cause it), as known (but then it functions as an object, and naming would be from the object), or as intended (but as intended it does not yet exist and has no causality).
claims: The end cannot cause the naming as acquired, as known, or as intended.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e464.summary: Reply: the division is insufficient; the end causes this distinction and naming insofar as it determines the object to cause the habit according to the requirement of the end.
claims: The end names the science by determining the object to cause the habit as the end requires.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e477.summary: Further objection: how can the end determine if it does not yet exist? Thomas acknowledges a singular difficulty, to be treated more fully at the beginning of Book 2. Briefly: although the end determining the object is not outside the intellect, there is a further end according to whose requirement the desire for this end is determined in us, and thus the object is determined to cause the habit by which we attain the end — e.g., the human being himself as more principal end determines what kind of speculation is needed and hence what speculable object begins the habit.
claims: A prior, more principal end determines our desire for the proximate end, which in turn determines the object.
The human being is the principal end in relation to which speculation is determined.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e524.summary: Alternatively, the end as intended causes this naming and distinction, and the proof is answered as just said.
claims: The end as intended can cause the science's distinction and naming.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e531.summary: Reply to the arguments for naming from the object: the major is true as to species and entity, but the object specifies neither habit nor act except in relation to the end; if absolved from the end's causality it would specify nothing; so since 'that because of which each thing is such is more so', the argument tells for the opposite. The same holds for the other two: as wood is called white from whiteness, not from the painter who causes it, a science is called speculative from speculation, not from its object.
claims: The object specifies a habit only in relation to the end.
A thing is named from its form (e.g., whiteness), not its efficient cause; a science is named from its end-act, not its object.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e568.summary: Article heading and question: what the proper end of theology is.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e576.summary: Thomas answers that the love (dilectio) of God, or affection, is the proper end of our theology. First argument: everything considered per se in theology is either to be used or to be enjoyed, and all such things are lovable; hence love is intended as the end throughout Scripture.
claims: The love of God is the proper end of our theology.
Everything treated in theology is a res utenda or fruenda and thus lovable.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e598.summary: Second argument: Scripture was given to join us spiritually to God, so theology intends above all that by which we are most intimately united to God, which is love; for every union of a rational creature to God is by intellect or will, and we are more perfectly united by the will, since the intellect's apprehension does not rest until the will rests in affection, and at least in this life we love more intimately than we understand — 'love enters where knowledge stays outside' (Hugh of St. Victor).
claims: Theology aims to unite us to God.
We are more perfectly united to God by will than by intellect.
In this life love reaches God more intimately than knowledge.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e630.summary: Third argument: theology's per se end is what directly orders us to eternal beatitude (Augustine, De Trin. 14), and this is the love of God, since according to Paul (1 Cor 13) neither speculation nor operation but charity alone avails per se for beatitude; all else avails only through charity.
claims: Charity alone avails per se for beatitude.
Speculation and good works are worthless without charity.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e679.summary: Fourth argument: although a science may have several ends, its principal end is that to which all others are ordered; in theology some parts intend speculation, others operation, but love is intended everywhere, and both speculation and operation are ordered to it.
claims: Speculation and operation in theology are both ordered to love as principal end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e694.summary: Supporting authority: Gregory on Ezekiel says that no passage of Scripture appears so cold literally that it does not appear fiery when struck by the spiritual sense.
claims: Every passage of Scripture, spiritually understood, enkindles love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e736.summary: Further authority: Augustine (De laude caritatis) says that if one cannot search all Scripture, one should hold charity, and one will hold both what one has learned and what one has not; charity is open in what one understands and hidden in what one does not.
claims: Charity contains the whole meaning of Scripture.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e737.summary: Further authority: Augustine (De doctrina christiana 1) concludes that the fullness and end of the law and of all Scripture is love of the thing to be enjoyed and of the one who can enjoy it with us.
claims: The end of all Scripture is love of God and neighbor.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e761.summary: Further authorities: Paul says 'the end of the commandment is charity' (1 Tim 1:5), and Christ, the highest doctor of theology, says the whole law and prophets depend on the two commandments of love of God and neighbor.
claims: Charity is the end of the commandment and the summary of the law.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e777.summary: Introduces objections: many argue against this truth in many ways, some directly, some indirectly; the direct arguments come first.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e785.summary: First direct objection: love would be either an intrinsic or extrinsic end of theology. Not intrinsic, since a habit's intrinsic end is the act it elicits, and love is elicited by charity, not theology. Not extrinsic, since a habit is named from its extrinsic end (as medicine is 'healing' from health), but theology cannot be named from love, since as object relates to object so act to act, and the object of one power names the object of another only accidentally (as white is accidentally sweet); love belongs to the will, theology to the intellect.
claims: Love is not the intrinsic end of theology, since theology does not elicit love.
An act of one power cannot name a habit of another power except accidentally.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e820.summary: Further direct objections: specifically different habits cannot have one proper end (though they may share a common end), and theology and charity differ specifically; love is the common end of every science, speculative (whose end is happiness, including delight and love, Ethics 10) and practical (moral science orders affection, and all appetite is love); and a habit's proper end cannot be present in one lacking the habit, yet many have charity without theology.
claims: Theology and charity, as specifically different habits, cannot share a proper end.
Love is the common end of all sciences and not proper to theology.
Many have charity without theology.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e885.summary: Further objection: no habit is perfectly present in one lacking its proper end; but someone lacking love could know the wayfarer's theology no less perfectly than one with charity.
claims: One without charity can know theology as perfectly as one with it.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e898.summary: Further objection: a habit's proper end is the proper act it elicits (Averroes, Metaph. 8; De caelo 2), and theology does not elicit love.
claims: A habit's proper end is its elicited act.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e929.summary: Further objection: if love were theology's end, God would not be its subject under the ratio of deity but as beloved or lovable, since the subject's ratio is taken in relation to the end; arguments that God is subject under the ratio of deity were given in q.1.
claims: If love were the end, God would be theology's subject as lovable, not as God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e955.summary: Thomas's response: the per se proper end of any habit is that by which its object is most perfectly attained, as speculation is the end of speculative science because the speculable is best attained by speculation; and the object of theology is most perfectly attained by love — a minor he will prove in Book 1 d.1 and at the end of Book 4, and here assumes.
claims: A habit's proper end is that by which its object is most perfectly attained.
Love attains the object of theology most perfectly.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e987.summary: Reply to the first objection: love is theology's extrinsic end. A habit is named not only from the act it elicits but also from the act to which it is per se ordered; the comparison of object to object holds only when one is per se ordered to the other. Theology does not elicit love but intends it and is per se ordered to it.
claims: Love is theology's extrinsic end.
A habit can be named from the act to which it is per se ordered, not only from its elicited act.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1009.summary: Reply to the second objection: there are two kinds of end — the finis quo, intrinsic, the act immediately elicited by the habit; and the finis cuius, extrinsic, that for the sake of which the agent acts.
claims: The end of a habit is either finis quo (intrinsic, elicited act) or finis cuius (extrinsic, what is aimed at).

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1027.summary: Continuation: the major holds of the same kind of end, but nothing prevents the same thing being the proper end of specifically different habits in different ways; the same act of love is the intrinsic finis quo of charity and the extrinsic finis cuius of theology, a distinction gathered from Aristotle (De anima 2; Physics 2).
claims: The act of love is charity's finis quo and theology's finis cuius.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1049.summary: Reply to the third objection: the same end taken the same way cannot be common to every science and proper to one. There are two delights following cognition: delight in the cognition itself (as in knowing a triangle) and delight in the known thing itself. The first is an end only when joined to the second; the second can be an end even of speculation. The first is found in every cognition and does not name a science; the second, principally and per se, only in theology. Likewise for love. The speculator's happiness as such consists in speculation, not the thing; and delight is the end of an operation only when the first is joined to the second.
claims: Delight in knowing differs from delight in the thing known.
Only delight and love directed to the thing itself can name a science, and this belongs per se to theology alone.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1123.summary: Possible reply to the argument from moral science: moral philosophy is ordered to love of creatures, theology principally to love of God.
claims: Moral science aims at love of creatures, theology at love of God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1134.summary: Objection to that reply: according to Cicero and Andronicus moral science is principally ordered to the worship of God, and so to the love of God, since true worship is true love (Augustine, City of God 10).
claims: Moral science is ordered to divine worship and so to love of God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1157.summary: Response: moral science, through the virtue philosophers call religion — a species of justice (Cicero, Andronicus) — promotes worship of God out of a debt of justice for benefits received, whereas theology promotes worship properly out of love.
claims: Philosophical religion worships God out of justice; theology does so out of love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1177.summary: Further objection: philosophers held God to be the ultimate end and highest good and so most to be loved, and to a benefactor one owes not only service but love.
claims: Philosophers also taught that God is to be loved most.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1190.summary: Reply to both: these arguments conclude about natural love, but theology's proper end is supernatural love; the whole argument equivocates on 'love' and hence on the consequent delight.
claims: Theology's end is supernatural love, distinct from the natural love philosophers recognized.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1206.summary: Reply to the fourth and fifth objections: they hold of the intrinsic end (finis quo), not the extrinsic (finis cuius); health, medicine's extrinsic end, can be in one without medicine and vice versa, and virtuous operation, the extrinsic end of moral science, can exist without it and vice versa.
claims: An extrinsic end can exist without the habit and the habit without it.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1232.summary: Reply to the sixth: the major is false, since praxis or operation is neither the proper act of moral science nor in the same power, yet is its proper end.
claims: The proper end of moral science is not its own elicited act.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1245.summary: The authorities cited in the proof, and all similar ones, are to be understood of the intrinsic finis quo, not the extrinsic finis cuius.
claims: Authorities identifying a habit's end with its act concern the finis quo.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1257.summary: Reply to the seventh: the consequent (that God is not subject under the ratio of deity) is not false.
claims: God is not the subject of theology under the absolute ratio of deity.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1266.summary: The proofs for the consequent's falsity were answered in q.1, where it was proved that God is not subject of theology under the absolute ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1277.summary: Introduces indirect arguments against the conclusion, drawn from the sayings of some.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1286.summary: First indirect argument: faith and theology are essentially one habit, so love is not theology's immediate end, since faith's immediate end is not love (its subject is God as first truth). Proof of the antecedent: as prudence in morals suffices both for the end and the means, so one habit in supernatural matters suffices for the articles (as faith) and the conclusions drawn from them (as theology).
claims: Faith and theology are essentially one habit.
Faith's subject is God as first truth, so its immediate end is not love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1321.summary: Further proofs: Aristotle (Ethics 6) lists the intellectual habits — understanding, science, wisdom, art, prudence, and (sometimes) faith, opinion, suspicion; theology is none but faith: not understanding (of immediate principles), not science (not demonstrative), not wisdom (which is understanding plus science), not art or prudence (about contingents), not opinion or suspicion (which involve fear). Further, habits with the same formal ratio of knowing are the same; faith and theology both tend to their object enigmatically and obscurely.
claims: Theology fits none of Aristotle's intellectual habits except faith.
Faith and theology share the formal ratio of knowing obscurely.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1384.summary: Further proof: the theological habit is neither inferior to faith (else in studying theology we would go from nobler to less noble) nor superior (since a habit of conclusions is not better known than a habit of principles, and the articles are theology's principles); so it is the same as faith.
claims: Theology can be neither inferior nor superior to faith, so it is identical with it.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1405.summary: Further proof: John 20:31, 'these things are written that you may believe and believing have life,' shows that the act of faith is theology's immediate end.
claims: Scripture is written so that we may believe.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1418.summary: Thomas argues that faith and theology differ really: one can exist without the other, since many have true faith without theology; having faith differs from giving an account of faith, which theology does (1 Pet 3:15); and habits regarding the same object under different formal rationes differ really — God is subject of faith as first truth, of theology as truly lovable.
claims: Faith and theology are really distinct habits.
Many believers lack theology.
Faith regards God as first truth, theology as the truly lovable.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1455.summary: Further argument: habits with different modes of tending to their objects differ really; by faith we tend to each article per se without resolving one into another, but by theology we deduce one truth syllogistically from another.
claims: Faith adheres to each article directly; theology deduces truths syllogistically.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1477.summary: Further argument: habits with formally different modes of generation differ really (Averroes, Metaph. 12); true faith, being infused, comes only by God's special influence, while theology, presupposing faith, can be had by teaching and human inquiry with only God's general influence.
claims: Faith is infused; theology is acquired through study with only God's general concurrence.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1499.summary: Thomas therefore denies the antecedent that faith and theology are one habit.
claims: Faith and theology are not one habit.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1508.summary: Replies to the proofs: the analogy with prudence actually tells against them — just as beyond prudence there is the scientific habit of the Ethics, so beyond faith there is theology, which conveys knowledge of credibles scientifically or quasi-scientifically. To the argument from Aristotle's list: q.2 showed theology is properly wisdom and in some way science; wisdom is not really understanding and science but resembles both, as theology does. To the third: obscurity is not of faith's formal ratio (q.3); Thomas marvels that so many doctors rely on this, since faith's light participates in spiritual light and darkness cannot be of light's formal ratio; likewise, no truthful habit can bring the intellect only obscurity, since every such habit participates in the first truth.
claims: Theology relates to faith as moral science to prudence.
Theology resembles both understanding and science.
Obscurity is not of the formal ratio of faith or theology.
Every truthful habit gives some knowledge, as every form gives some actuality.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1613.summary: Reply to the fourth: faith, as supernaturally infused, is prior in dignity to theology and every acquired virtue, but studying theology does not move from nobler to less noble, since faith is not lost when theology is gained; as happiness united with prudence is more choiceworthy (Ethics 1), faith with theology is more worthy than faith alone.
claims: Faith is nobler than theology, but faith with theology is nobler than faith alone.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1642.summary: Reply to the fifth: John says Scripture was written that we may believe because theology was written to defend faith against the impious and nourish it in the good.
claims: Theology serves to defend and nourish faith.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1655.summary: Others argue indirectly that knowledge of God is theology's end: the end of a science's principles is the end of the science, since principles implicitly contain the whole science; and the end of the articles of faith, theology's principles, is knowledge of God.
claims: The end of the articles of faith, knowledge of God, is the end of theology.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1677.summary: Second argument: not every last thing but the best has the ratio of end (Physics 2), and knowledge of God is the noblest act of the rational soul intended in theology.
claims: Knowledge of God is the best act and therefore the end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1690.summary: Further arguments: the contemplative life is nobler than the active, so speculation is nobler than operation and is theology's end; and the proper end of wisdom is speculation (Metaph. 1, 8; Ethics 10), while theology is properly wisdom.
claims: The contemplative life is nobler than the active.
Wisdom's end is speculation, and theology is wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1708.summary: Further arguments: some say the end is not knowledge in this life but in the fatherland ('Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God'); among ordered habits, the highest end belongs to the highest habit, and the highest end, eternal beatitude, consists principally in seeing God; and the subject of a science as imperfectly known is its end as perfectly known, so perfect knowledge of God is theology's end.
claims: The vision of God in the fatherland is theology's end.
Beatitude consists principally in the vision of God.
The subject imperfectly known becomes the end when perfectly known.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1746.summary: Further argument: Augustine (sermon on Jacob and Esau) says all our work in this life is to purify the mind's eye that God may be seen; mysteries are celebrated and the word preached for this.
claims: All the Church's activity aims at the vision of God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1770.summary: Thomas rejects these: what among all human possibilities in this life and the next is best, and so the end, is that in which merit principally consists in the way and reward in the fatherland; this is the love of God. Merit consists principally in what alone suffices for merit whatever else is posited or removed — charity, without which every virtue is dead and formless, while charity alone cannot be formless. The reward will be treated at d.1 on fruition.
claims: The love of God is the best human act, in which merit and reward principally consist.
Charity alone makes virtues meritorious and cannot itself be formless.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1805.summary: Reply to the first: the end of the principles may be the mediate, remote end of the science but not its immediate, proximate end; and the minor is false, since even through knowledge of the articles we intend the love of God, without which faith is dead and formless.
claims: The end of principles is only the remote end of the science.
Even knowledge of the articles is ordered to love, without which faith is dead.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1823.summary: Reply to the second: the minor is false, as already shown and to be shown further.
claims: Knowledge of God is not the noblest act; love is.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1832.summary: Reply to the third: it shows only that speculative is nobler than practical; but whatever meritorious dignity belongs to contemplative and active life belongs to them as ordered to the affective, as both speculation and action are finally ordered to love of God.
claims: The merit of both contemplative and active lives derives from their ordering to love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1852.summary: Reply to the fourth: the major holds of philosophical, naturally discovered wisdom, not theological wisdom. Alternatively, since wisdom is 'savory science', although it intends speculation it more principally intends love, since mental savor and delight arise more properly from love than from speculation.
claims: Philosophical wisdom aims at speculation, theological wisdom at love.
Wisdom's savor comes more from love than from speculation.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1875.summary: Reply to the fifth and sixth: the vision of the fatherland is theology's remote end, but the question concerns the proper and immediate end, from which a science is named. Moreover, they assume falsely, since both in this life and the next love is nobler than speculation, and beatitude consists more in love than in speculation.
claims: The vision of God is only the remote end of the wayfarer's theology.
Beatitude consists more in love than in vision.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1897.summary: The seventh argument is answered in the same way.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1904.summary: Reply to the eighth (Augustine on the mind's eye): Augustine understands the eye as our intention (as in his Sermon on the Mount on Matt 6:22), and intention is purified far more by the love of God than by speculation; so Augustine supports Thomas's view.
claims: The mind's 'eye' in Augustine is intention, which love purifies more than speculation.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1936.summary: Introduces another indirect line: that praxis or operation is theology's end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1945.summary: First argument: the Savior said, 'If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments' (Matt 19:17), and keeping the commandments consists in moral works.
claims: Keeping the commandments, i.e., moral works, is required for salvation.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1956.summary: Second argument: a science whose common conceptions are nearly all moral has praxis as end; theology proceeds from such conceptions — God is good, God is to be loved, evil is to be avoided and good done.
claims: Theology's common conceptions are moral principles, so its end is praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1981.summary: Third argument: a science that mostly treats of morals has praxis as end; theology almost everywhere treats the formation of morals.
claims: Theology chiefly treats morals and so aims at praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e1994.summary: If one answers that these are not intended for their own sake but to order us to the love of God, these opponents grant it but add that love itself is truly praxis, which they prove in several ways, beginning with a definition.
claims: Some hold that love of God is itself praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2014.summary: Their definition (Scotus's): praxis is an operation of a power other than the intellect, naturally posterior to understanding, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason so as to be right; all parts of this definition fit the love of God, so it is true praxis.
claims: Praxis is an act of a non-intellectual power, posterior to understanding, apt to conform to right reason.
The love of God satisfies this definition.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2027.summary: Further arguments: if love of the ultimate end were not praxis, some operation in human power would be neither praxis nor speculation; and every act of the will is praxis. They add that both acts elicited by the will and acts commanded by it are praxis — elicited acts like loving and willing primarily and per se, commanded acts secondarily.
claims: Every act of the will is praxis, primarily if elicited, secondarily if commanded.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2058.summary: Thomas rejects this: an act that is neither choice nor follows choice is not praxis (Averroes: praxis is operation according to choice); love of God is not choice, since will is of the end and choice of means, and choice concludes deliberation about contingent means, whereas love of God tends immediately to the ultimate end. Further, if something not operable by us were praxis, the practical/speculative distinction would collapse, since the practical concerns what we can make; but meritorious love of God is not operable by us, being infused charity — otherwise we could be saved by pure natural powers, which is heretical (Titus 3:5).
claims: Praxis involves choice, which concerns means, while love of God concerns the end.
Meritorious love of God is infused, not operable by us.
Claiming we can produce meritorious love by nature is heretical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2117.summary: Further: the opponent himself says an act not in our power is not praxis, but meritorious love of God is not in our power, otherwise the Pelagian error would return.
claims: Meritorious love is not in our power, so on the opponent's own terms it is not praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2131.summary: Further: an act whose direction does not fall under the human intellect is not praxis; love of God requires a supernatural director ('those led by the Spirit of God are sons of God,' Rom 8:14).
claims: Love of God requires supernatural direction beyond human reason, so it is not praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2149.summary: Reply to the first argument about praxis: the definition is insufficient, omitting what principally belongs to praxis, namely being operable by us or in our power; and the minor is false, since conformity to our reason does not suffice to direct this supernatural act.
claims: The definition of praxis omits that praxis must be in our power.
Human reason does not suffice to direct supernatural love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2167.summary: Reply to the second: Thomas denies the consequence, since the love in question is not in our power; nor is the consequent unfitting, if 'operation' is taken broadly for any act elicited by a human.
claims: Supernatural love is neither praxis nor speculation, and this is not absurd.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2187.summary: Reply to the third: Thomas denies the major and the addition; not every act elicited by the will is praxis (as with love of God), nor every act commanded by the will, since then the intellect's speculative act, being commanded by the will, would be praxis — which the opponent himself denies in his writing.
claims: Not every act elicited or commanded by the will is praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2205.summary: Article heading and question: whether the theology of the wayfarer is properly called affective.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2214.summary: Restates the question of Article 3: whether the science of sacred Scripture is properly called affective.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2226.summary: Thomas answers: since Article 1 proved that a science is named from its end and Article 2 that the end of theology is the love of God, theology is properly called dilective or affective. Further, the noblest science should be named from the noblest end; theology, being properly wisdom, is the noblest science, and love of God is the noblest end, since no gift of God is more excellent (Augustine).
claims: Theology is properly called affective or dilective.
The noblest science is named from the noblest end, the love of God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2267.summary: Second argument: a habit whose proper end can be reduced neither to speculation nor to praxis belongs to a third genus; theology's end, love of God, is neither speculation (being nobler) nor praxis (its object not being operable by us); so since all things are named from their end, theology is affective.
claims: Theology belongs to a third genus of science, neither speculative nor practical.
Love of God is neither speculation nor praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2293.summary: Objections to a third genus. First: as naturally acquired scientific habits relate to natural love, so theology relates to supernatural love; but no naturally acquired scientific habit is ordered to or named from natural love; so neither theology from supernatural love.
claims: Natural sciences are not named from natural love, so theology should not be named from supernatural love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2313.summary: Second objection: every science is either for its own sake (speculative) or not (practical), so there is no third genus.
claims: Every science is either for its own sake or for another's.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2324.summary: Third objection: according to Avicenna (Metaph. 1), speculative science concerns what is not operable by us and practical what is operable; every being is one or the other, so every science is speculative or practical.
claims: Every being is operable or not by us, so every science is practical or speculative.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2343.summary: Fourth objection: philosophers adequately distinguished the sciences and never mentioned an affective science.
claims: The philosophers' division of sciences includes no affective science.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2353.summary: Fifth objection: every science attains its object either by an act consisting in knowledge of truth alone (speculative) or by exercise of external work (practical).
claims: Sciences attain their objects either by knowledge or by external work.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2366.summary: Sixth objection: theology's end is either knowledge of truth about charity (merely speculative) or knowledge of how charity can be had in us (merely practical).
claims: Theology about charity is either speculative or practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2379.summary: Thomas responds that since, according to the saints, theology's final intention is to join and unite us intimately to God, it should be named from that by which we are most nobly and intimately united to him — charity or love. Though we become like God by knowledge (1 John 3:2), by charity and love we are graciously transformed into God, as Dionysius says love, if strong, makes ecstasy and transforms the lover into the beloved; Augustine and Hugh (De arrha animae) agree.
claims: Theology should be named from that which most intimately unites us to God.
Knowledge assimilates us to God, but love transforms us into God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2425.summary: Reply to the first objection: the analogy is to be denied, since the natural love philosophers discussed is love of creatures, which is not dignified enough to name a science.
claims: Natural love of creatures is not dignified enough to name a science.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2441.summary: Explanation: in understanding things move to the soul, but in loving the soul moves to the things loved (De anima). Things, however lowly, are ennobled when understood, constituted in spiritual being; but the soul, however noble, is usually debased when it loves creatures for their own sake through the lover's transformation into the beloved; conversely, loving God above all and neighbor for God, it is wondrously ennobled. So natural love of creatures is not intended as the end of humanly acquired science, but love of God, owing to its dignity, is intended per se and names the science.
claims: In knowing, things come to the soul; in loving, the soul goes to things.
Loving creatures for themselves debases the soul; loving God ennobles it.
Love of God's dignity makes it apt to name a science.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2480.summary: Reply to the second objection: the philosopher who made this division knew no inner act nobler than speculation nor outer act nobler than virtuous operation, so the division seemed sufficient to him. But we hold that meritorious love of God in this life and rewarding love in the next is nobler than all speculation and virtuous operation, so the science that per se and principally intends it is named from it.
claims: Philosophers knew nothing nobler than speculation and virtuous operation.
Meritorious love of God surpasses both, warranting a third, affective kind of science.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2505.summary: Replies to the third, fourth and fifth: the same answer applies; the fifth's division is insufficient, since theology attains its object neither by knowledge alone nor by practical direction, but principally and most nobly by supernatural love.
claims: Theology attains its object principally by supernatural love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2523.summary: Reply to the sixth: the division is likewise insufficient, since theology's end is neither knowledge of truth nor practical knowledge but charity itself.
claims: Theology's end is charity itself.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2534.summary: Article heading: in Article 4, motives of various opinions that seem to oppose the truth of Article 3 are to be removed.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2550.summary: Thomas sorts the opposing opinions into three general types: theology is simply speculative; simply practical; or both — subdivided into qualifiedly speculative and simply practical, qualifiedly practical and simply speculative, and simply both. He will state and solve their motives briefly.
claims: Opposing views hold theology to be speculative, practical, or both in various combinations.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2583.summary: First argument of those holding theology simply speculative: a science whose per se principal end is knowledge of God is simply speculative (Metaph. 2: theory's end is truth, practice's work), and theology is such, by the arguments for speculation as its end given in Article 2.
claims: Theology's end is knowledge of God, so it is speculative.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2624.summary: Second argument: the noblest science should be speculative, since Ethics 6 shows wisdom nobler than prudence, the speculative intellect being better than the practical (Averroes); theology is noblest.
claims: The noblest science must be speculative, since speculation is nobler than praxis.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2628.summary: Third argument: our theology resembles the theology of God and the blessed, which is speculative.
claims: Our theology imitates the speculative theology of God and the blessed.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2655.summary: Fourth argument: a habit having the ratio of wisdom is truly and simply speculative, and theology is truly wisdom.
claims: Wisdom is speculative, and theology is wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2664.summary: Fifth argument: a science of what is not operable by us is simply speculative, and theology is such. Thomas's general response: speculation does not name a science when it is ordered to a further end per se intended by the science, and theology's speculation is so ordered.
claims: A science of the non-operable is speculative.
Speculation does not name a science when ordered to a further end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2657.summary: Reply to the first argument: the minor is false.
claims: Knowledge of God is not theology's per se principal end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2687.summary: Reply to the second: the major is false, since affective is nobler than speculative. The philosophers knew no love nobler than speculation and serving as its end; had they known one, they would have posited an affective science ordering speculation to such love.
claims: Affective knowledge is nobler than speculative.
Philosophers would have posited an affective science had they known such love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2683.summary: Reply to the third: the theology of the fatherland is better called amative or fruitive than speculative.
claims: The theology of the blessed is fruitive rather than speculative.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2692.summary: Explanation: though theology of the way and the fatherland can both be named from love, charity and dilection, the wayfarer's theology is properly named from affection, which signifies imperfect love in desire with mobility and instability, fitting an imperfect theology; the fatherland's from fruition, perfect and stable love, fitting a perfect theology ordered to heavenly love as its proximate end. Charity, love and dilection, being taken perfectly or imperfectly, can name both. Reply to the fourth: the major holds if wisdom consists in speculation as an end not further ordered, which is not so in our theology.
claims: The wayfarer's theology is properly called affective, the theology of the blessed fruitive.
Affection is imperfect, unstable love; fruition is perfect, restful love.
Wisdom is speculative only if its speculation is not ordered to a further end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2749.summary: Reply to the fifth: a science of the non-operable is speculative if its speculation is not ordered to another end per se intended in it, but theology's speculation is ordered to love.
claims: Theology's speculation is ordered to love and so does not make it speculative.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2762.summary: Arguments of those holding theology simply practical: a science whose proper end is praxis is practical, and praxis is theology's end (per earlier arguments); faith is a practical habit, ordered not only to believing but to loving what is believed, and theology is founded on faith; and knowledge directing the will lest it err is practical, and theology directs us in loving the ultimate end, where one may err by using what is to be enjoyed. Others agreeing in the conclusion add, against the doctor who restricts the practical to directing another power, that logic, rhetoric and all intellectual habits directing acts of other habits within the intellect are properly practical — rhetoric being an active virtue; logic having priority, conformity, activity and direction over other sciences; existing not for its own sake but for the acts it directs; extending beyond its own act; being divided into docens and utens; and making its objects (propositions, syllogisms). Hence their general rule: every habit having as its end not only its elicited act but the act it directs, in whatever power, is truly practical.
claims: Theology's end is praxis, so it is practical.
Faith is practical, ordered to loving what is believed.
Knowledge that directs the will is practical.
Logic and rhetoric are practical habits because they direct other intellectual acts.
Any habit whose end includes the act it directs is practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2900.summary: A further group (following the preceding) posits four conclusions, the first being that the wayfarer's theology is properly practical, since it regulates the will's act concerning divine things and directs external acts to divine worship (latria).
claims: The wayfarer's theology is practical because it regulates the will and directs worship.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2918.summary: Their second conclusion: the theology of the blessed is practical, since it has priority to and conformity with the will's act toward the beatific object, the will loving it as the intellect foreknows it is to be loved.
claims: The theology of the blessed is practical because it directs the will's love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2934.summary: Their third conclusion: God's theology of necessary things is practical, since as God knows himself to be loved he loves himself, and if per impossibile he loved otherwise his act would be disordered, contrary to right reason; so his appetite is regulated by reason.
claims: God's knowledge of necessary truths is practical, as it regulates his self-love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2950.summary: Their fourth conclusion: God's theology of contingents, such as the Incarnation, is not practical, since the divine intellect does not regulate God's will about such things; were it a determinate rule while the will is open to opposites, the will could sin by deviating from it.
claims: God's knowledge of contingents is not practical because his intellect does not rule his will in contingent matters.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e2968.summary: Thomas first rejects their shared principal conclusion: if our theology were simply practical, some naturally acquired habit would be nobler than theology, since speculative habits are nobler than practical (Metaph. 1, 9) and many natural habits are speculative; and they themselves call theology properly wisdom, while a practical wisdom is a contradiction in terms, wisdom's end not being praxis (Ethics 6, 10). Reply to the first argument: the minor is false and its proofs fail.
claims: If theology were simply practical, some natural speculative habit would be nobler than theology.
A practical wisdom is a contradiction in terms.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3010.summary: Reply to the second: the major is false; even if its proof were true, it would show only that faith is affective, not practical, and the same holds of theology.
claims: Faith's ordering to love makes it affective, not practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3024.summary: Reply to the third: not every knowledge directing the will lest it err is practical, only that directing it about contingents operable by us. Moreover, although theology directs us somewhat toward love of the ultimate end, the sufficient director of that love, as theology's end, is God alone, since such love is meritorious and not in our power.
claims: Only direction of the will regarding contingent operables is practical.
God alone sufficiently directs meritorious love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3048.summary: Against the others' claim that directing another habit's act makes a science practical: then metaphysics would be most practical, since it directs and rectifies the principles of all sciences (Metaph. 4), yet it is supremely speculative.
claims: Metaphysics directs all sciences yet is speculative, so direction does not make a habit practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3068.summary: Second: the habit of principles (intellectus) would be practical, since it directs science's act regarding conclusions.
claims: The habit of first principles directs science but is not practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3079.summary: Third: every subalternating science would be practical, since it directs the subalternate science, whose evidence of principles depends on it; but this is false, since nothing prevents a subalternate science being speculative, and then a speculative science would depend on a practical one or be nobler than it, both unfitting.
claims: Subalternating sciences direct subalternate ones without being practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3099.summary: Reply to the first argument about rhetoric: Aristotle calls rhetoric a virtue but not an active virtue; even if he did, it can be glossed as 'factive' because it makes rhetorical persuasions; Averroes's 'faculty' is to be read likewise.
claims: Rhetoric is called a virtue but not an active (practical) one.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3121.summary: Reply to the second (logic's priority, conformity, activity and direction): these do not suffice to make a directing habit practical unless the directed act in some way makes the object of the directing habit; logic directs natural philosophy's act, but that act does not make logic's subject, so the intended end does not go beyond speculation.
claims: A directing habit is practical only if the directed act produces the directing habit's object.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3144.summary: Reply to the third: the ratio of a practical habit consists not in directing any act but in directing an act that makes the subject of the directing habit. In a practical habit the elicited and directed acts concern the same object, constituted in being by the directed act — as moral philosophy directs acts that cause good morals, and medicine acts that cause health. Logic as docens already possesses its subject before as utens it directs other sciences.
claims: A practical habit directs acts that produce its own subject, as in ethics and medicine.
Logica docens presupposes its subject before logica utens directs other sciences.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3190.summary: Anticipated objection: at least logica utens would be practical. Thomas denies it: then every science would be practical, an unheard-of absurdity, since every science attains its object only through acts of logica utens (defining, enunciating, syllogizing, dividing). To the claim that logic is for another's sake while speculative science is for its own: if directing another habit made a habit for another's sake, metaphysics would be too, since Metaph. 4 teaches how it proves the principles of all sciences.
claims: If logica utens were practical, every science would be practical.
Directing other sciences does not make metaphysics or logic 'for another's sake'.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3238.summary: Thomas distinguishes two kinds of direction: from the indigence of the directing habit, which belongs to practical habits, since they cannot sufficiently attain their subject by their own elicited act but must direct another power's act that makes it — so their speculating is for directing and directing for making, and they depend on what they direct; and from sufficiency, which leaves a habit maximally speculative, since what it directs depends on it rather than vice versa. Logic directs the other sciences in the second way, being prior to them; hence it is unfitting to seek science and the mode of knowing together (Metaph. 2), the mode of knowing being logic, which must be learned first.
claims: Direction from indigence makes a habit practical; direction from sufficiency leaves it speculative.
Logic directs other sciences from sufficiency and is prior to them.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3295.summary: Anticipated objection: no habit can exist without its subject, so no habit can direct an act that makes its subject, since acting presupposes being and of a subject we presuppose that it is and what it is (Post. An. 1).
claims: A habit presupposes its subject and so cannot direct the act that produces it.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3319.summary: Reply: a subject's being can mean its actual existence or its essential being contained perfectly in its proximate causes. The antecedent is false in the first sense, true in the second; as science remains when its subject is destroyed in actual existence but remains in its causes, so a scientific habit can be acquired before its subject actually exists — as Noah, first planter of the vine, knowing its causes, could conceive a habit whose subject was the vine existing in its causes and which directed his acts producing the actual vine. Aristotle's dictum concerns speculative science, or else we presuppose that the subject is either in itself or in its proximate causes. Reply to the fourth: extension makes a habit practical only if it arises from indigence.
claims: A subject may exist in its proximate causes before actually existing.
A practical habit can direct the production of its own subject's actual existence.
Extension beyond its act makes a habit practical only when arising from indigence.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3408.summary: Reply to the fifth (division into docens and utens): the major is false, since metaphysics too is sometimes utens, as in Physics 1 when the natural philosopher puts on the metaphysician's habit to prove natural philosophy's principles against Parmenides and Melissus.
claims: Metaphysics too has a utens mode without being practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3425.summary: Reply to the sixth (logic makes its objects): the major holds when the object is real, but not when it is a being of reason within the intellect, since a habit becomes practical by extension (De anima 3) and there is no extension in producing an object remaining in the same power. Alternatively, the minor is false: regarding a syllogism or proposition there is a productive act and a considerative act; the first naturally precedes and belongs to the intellect, not to logic; logic presupposes its object as made — just as a science of scientific habits would presuppose rather than produce them. The same applies to rhetoric, and their general rule is false.
claims: Producing a being of reason within the intellect does not make a habit practical.
Logic considers, but does not produce, syllogisms and propositions.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3482.summary: Regarding the third doctor's four conclusions: the first three are false, since neither the wayfarer's theology, nor the blessed's, nor God's of necessary things makes its object; and a science is practical because its object is operable by us, as philosophers and theologians agree.
claims: The first three of the four conclusions fail because none of these theologies makes its object.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3502.summary: The doctor's reply: since volition is an operation, by the locus a coniugatis whatever is volible by us is operable by us; hence theology, though of eternal things, can be practical, since eternal things are volible and so in some way operable.
claims: By the topic from conjugates, what is volible is operable, so theology of eternal things can be practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3520.summary: Thomas calls this a most simplistic response from so great a doctor, for the following reasons.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3529.summary: First: contingents are volible and operable by God, so God would have practical science of contingents, contradicting the doctor's fourth conclusion.
claims: The doctor's reply contradicts his fourth conclusion.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3542.summary: Second: every speculative science would be practical, since no object is so speculable that it is not volible — indeed nothing could be stably speculated without the will's intention.
claims: On the doctor's principle every speculative science would be practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3559.summary: Further: formality and form are no less conjugates than operation and operable, yet the doctor in his first question denies that 'formality, therefore form' or 'many formalities, therefore many forms' follow, comparing it to 'many essentials, therefore many essences'. Why accept the locus a coniugatis here and reject it there? In truth it holds in both places, so it is wrongly denied there — though here it does not prove his point. The essential/essence instance fails, since divine essentials are distinguished only by reason; but the doctor posits formalities formally distinct, not merely by reason, and so must posit many forms. Also, not every operation and operable makes a habit practical, but only one that constitutes the operable in being, while the volible precedes volition. The motives of the first three conclusions fail since regulation and direction do not suffice. Thomas leaves the fourth conclusion undetermined, but if any divine knowledge is practical, it is more that of contingents and creatures than of the necessary creative essence; nor does the doctor's motive hold, since in God, as in us, the will can will nothing the intellect does not first (in reason) know, so although God's will is free toward opposites in producing contingents, it produces only as it has eternally disposed in knowing.
claims: The locus a coniugatis is valid in both contexts, so the doctor inconsistently rejects it for formalities.
If formalities are formally distinct, there must be many forms.
Only an operation that constitutes the operable in being makes a habit practical.
If any divine knowledge is practical, it is that of contingent creatures.
In God the will wills nothing the intellect does not first know.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3681.summary: Introduces a third opinion contrary to Article 3: theology is simply speculative and simply practical.
claims: Some hold theology to be both simply speculative and simply practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3692.summary: First argument: a habit treating speculables (God, separate substances) more perfectly than metaphysics and morals and virtues more perfectly than ethics is both speculative and practical; theology is such.
claims: Theology surpasses both metaphysics and ethics, so it is both speculative and practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3708.summary: Second argument: a habit that is both wisdom considering eternal reasons and science administering temporal things is both speculative and practical (Augustine, De Trin. 14).
claims: Theology is both sapientia of eternal things and scientia of temporal administration.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3734.summary: Third argument: a science intending speculation for its own sake and operation for its own sake is simply both; theology is such, since a science of all our duties would still need one of speculating about God, and vice versa, and right operation is necessary for eternal life ('keep the commandments').
claims: Theology intends both speculation and operation for their own sakes.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3773.summary: Fourth argument: a science whose ratio of considering comprehends both speculables and agibles is both; theology's formal ratio of considering is the revealable, and both speculables and agibles are revealed.
claims: Theology's formal ratio, the revealable, covers both speculables and agibles.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3792.summary: Fifth argument: God's science is one and both practical (regarding what he makes) and speculative (regarding himself), and our theology, as its image, should conform to it.
claims: Our theology, imaging God's, is both practical and speculative.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3808.summary: Sixth argument: the faithful are no less provided for than the gentiles, who have purely speculative sciences for the contemplative life and purely active ones for the active life; since theology directs Christians in both, it is both.
claims: Theology must serve both contemplative and active life, as pagan sciences do separately.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3830.summary: Thomas rejects this: sciences are distinguished principally and per se by ends and objects, so with two ends, speculating and operating, theology would not be one science. Confirmation: sciences are diversified by diverse objective rationes, and since the objective ratio is always taken in relation to the end, two ends would mean two objective rationes.
claims: Two proper ends would make theology two sciences.
The objective ratio is taken in relation to the end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3856.summary: Some of them reply that despite these two ends, theology is one habit by being bound together by one extrinsic end, eternal life.
claims: Theology is unified by its single remote end, eternal life.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3869.summary: Thomas rejects this: that is a remote end commonly intended by every true science, to which all are ultimately ordered; if it unified theology despite diverse proximate ends, by parity all sciences would be one science.
claims: A common remote end cannot unify a science, otherwise all sciences would be one.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3889.summary: Further: if theology were both speculative and practical, theology would differ more from itself than natural philosophy from metaphysics or mathematics, since things placed under two members of a division differ more than those under one, and the latter three are all speculative.
claims: A theology both speculative and practical would differ more from itself than distinct speculative sciences do from each other.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3919.summary: Further: two essential differences dividing a genus cannot belong to the same species; practical and speculative are essential differences dividing the genus of science, of which theology is a species. Thomas notes this tells directly against them but concerns him only insofar as it might tell against him, since unlike them he does not hold every science to be practical or speculative, positing a third, affective genus.
claims: Opposed essential differences cannot belong to one species.
Thomas posits a third, affective genus of science.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3950.summary: Further: a science is one that is of one genus of subject (Post. An. 1), but the speculable and the operable are not one subject.
claims: Speculables and operables do not form one subject-genus.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3961.summary: Their reply: they can be called one subject because of one ratio of considering, the revealable.
claims: The revealable unifies theology's subject.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3972.summary: Thomas rejects this: if there were one formal ratio of considering with diverse ends, there would be less unity in the end than in what is for the end, which is impossible.
claims: Unity in means cannot exceed unity in the end.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e3985.summary: Reply to their first argument: the major holds if the science rests finally in speculation of speculables and the operation of morals; but though theology treats both more perfectly, it does not rest in them but refers both to the love of God.
claims: Theology refers both speculation and moral operation to the love of God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e4003.summary: Reply to the second: both the speculation of wisdom and the administration of science must be referred to love as the per se end of theology, from which it is named.
claims: Both wisdom's speculation and science's administration are ordered to love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e4020.summary: Reply to the third: many deny the minor — speculative theorists say operation is for the sake of speculation, practical theorists the reverse — but even granting neither is for the other, both are for the sake of loving God, without which each is vain and frustrated of its end.
claims: Both speculation and operation are for the sake of loving God, without which they are vain.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e4044.summary: Reply to the fourth: the major holds only if both action and speculation are not referred to a further end, such as love of God.
claims: Comprehending speculables and agibles does not make a science both if both are ordered to love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e4055.summary: Reply to the fifth: just as God knows himself first and principally and creatures consequently, so even if his science were practical and speculative it would not be equally so, but principally speculative and consequently practical — which tells against the opponent's conclusion that our theology is simply both.
claims: God's science, if both, is principally speculative and only consequently practical.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e4075.summary: Reply to the sixth: we are better provided for by the one science of theology than the gentiles by many; yet it is properly neither speculative nor practical, though it retains the power of both, since as both active and contemplative life per se intend the love of God, so theology, directing us in both, intends that love and is rightly named from it.
claims: Theology serves both lives better than many pagan sciences while being properly neither speculative nor practical.
Both active and contemplative life intend the love of God.

HuYgTa-d1e964-d1e4099.summary: Reply to the principal argument: although a science is not named from an act of the will as its intrinsic finis quo, it can be named from it as its finis cuius.
claims: A science can be named from an act of the will as its finis cuius.

HuYgTa-d1e964-Dd1e751.summary: Article 4: removing the motives of opinions opposed to Article 3. Thomas classifies opponents as holding theology simply speculative, simply practical, or both. Against the speculative view he argues that theology's speculation is ordered to love, and that the theology of the blessed is fruitive. Against the practical view he denies that directing another habit's act makes a habit practical — otherwise metaphysics, the habit of principles and subalternating sciences would be practical — and defines a practical habit as one directing acts that produce its own subject from indigence (illustrated by Noah and the vine), so that logic and rhetoric are not practical. He rejects Scotus's four conclusions and his use of the locus a coniugatis, charging inconsistency with his doctrine of formalities. Against the view that theology is both, he argues that two proper ends would destroy its unity, and that both speculation and operation are ordered to the love of God.
claims: Theology's speculation is ordered to love, so it is not speculative.
A habit is practical only if, from indigence, it directs acts producing its own subject.
Logic, rhetoric and metaphysics are not practical even though they direct other acts.
Scotus's argument from the locus a coniugatis is inconsistent with his treatment of formalities.
Theology cannot be both speculative and practical without losing its unity.
The wayfarer's theology is affective, the theology of the blessed fruitive.

HuYgTa-d1e964-Dd1e617.summary: Article 3: whether the wayfarer's theology is properly affective. Thomas concludes from the first two articles that theology, named from its end, the love of God, is properly affective or dilective — a third genus of science, since love is neither speculation nor praxis. He answers objections that every science is speculative or practical by noting that philosophers knew no act nobler than speculation and virtuous operation, while meritorious love of God surpasses both; he argues that love, which transforms the lover into God, is what most intimately unites us to God, and that love of God, unlike natural love of creatures, ennobles the soul.
claims: Theology is properly affective or dilective.
There is a third genus of science beyond speculative and practical.
Love transforms the lover into the beloved and unites us most intimately to God.
Philosophers' division of sciences was incomplete because they did not know supernatural love.

HuYgTa-d1e964-Dd1e582.summary: Article 2: what the proper end of theology is. Thomas holds that the love of God is theology's proper end, since all its matter is lovable, love unites us most intimately to God, charity alone avails for beatitude, and speculation and operation in theology are ordered to love, as Gregory, Augustine, Paul and Christ attest. He answers direct objections through the distinction between charity's intrinsic finis quo and theology's extrinsic finis cuius, distinguishing supernatural from natural love. He refutes indirect arguments that faith and theology are one habit, that knowledge or vision of God is theology's end (love is nobler, and merit and reward consist principally in it), and that praxis is its end — rejecting Scotus's definition of praxis because meritorious love is neither chosen nor in our power.
claims: The love of God is the proper end of theology.
Love is theology's finis cuius, though charity's finis quo.
Theology's end is supernatural, not natural, love.
Faith and theology are really distinct habits.
Love is nobler than knowledge, and merit and reward consist principally in it.
Meritorious love of God is not praxis, being neither chosen nor in our power.

HuYgTa-d1e964-Dd1e186.summary: Article 1: from what a science is properly named. Against those who name sciences from their objects, Thomas argues that a science is named from its end: the same object can be treated by practical and speculative sciences; Aristotle distinguishes them by ends; the object causes only as moved by the end; and God can supply an object's causality but not separate a science from its end. He explains that the end names the science by determining the object to cause the habit, and that objects specify habits only in relation to ends.
claims: A science is properly named from its end, not its object.
The object specifies a habit only as determined by the end.
God can supply the causality of the object but not of the end.

HuYgTa-d1e964.summary: Prologue, Question 4: whether the theology of the wayfarer is properly called affective. Thomas argues that a science is named from its end rather than its object; that the proper end of theology is the love of God, by which we are most intimately united to God and in which merit and reward principally consist; and that theology is therefore properly 'affective' or 'dilective', a third genus of science beyond the speculative and practical. Using the distinction between a habit's intrinsic finis quo and extrinsic finis cuius, he shows that love, elicited by charity, can be theology's end; he distinguishes theology from faith; and he refutes those who make knowledge, vision or praxis its end, including Scotus's account of praxis. In the final article he answers those who hold theology speculative, practical (including arguments that logic is practical and Scotus's four conclusions), or both, arguing that a practical habit must direct acts that produce its own subject and that every theological activity, speculative or practical, is ordered to the love of God.
claims: A science is named from its end.
The proper end of the wayfarer's theology is the love of God.
Theology is properly affective, a third genus of science, neither speculative nor practical.
Love is theology's extrinsic finis cuius, though charity elicits it.
Faith and theology are really distinct habits.
A habit is practical only if it directs acts productive of its own subject.
The wayfarer's theology is affective, the theology of the blessed fruitive.
